notes.summary: Data Interpretation gives a table or chart followed by questions on totals, averages, percentages, ratios and central angles. Expect 2 to 4 questions in Tier 1 and 3 to 5 in Tier 2. The maths is easy; the marks are lost by misreading units or rows and by slow division, so these notes focus on reading carefully and calculating with fractions.

concepts.title: What a DI set looks like
concepts.body:
Data Interpretation (DI) gives you some data, usually a table, a bar graph, a line graph or a pie chart, followed by a few questions on it. The maths is simple: totals, averages, percentages and ratios. What makes DI hard is reading the data correctly and calculating fast.

A good routine for every set:

  1. Read the title and the units first (thousands, lakhs, crores, percent, degrees).
  2. Check what each row, column, bar or line stands for. Read the legend.
  3. Read the question and write down only the numbers it needs.
  4. Glance at the options. If they are far apart, round the numbers and estimate.

concepts.title: Tables
concepts.body:
A table gives exact numbers, so most table questions need exact answers. Tips:

  • If several questions use row or column totals, find them once and write them beside the table.
  • Read the header carefully. "Marks obtained (in %)" with maximum marks in brackets means you must convert: 72% of a 150-mark paper is 108 marks.
  • When a question names two years, put your finger on both cells before calculating. Mixing up rows is the most common DI mistake.

Mini example: if a table shows sales of 120, 80, 150 and 100 for four shops, the total is 450 and the average is 112.5.

concepts.title: Bar graphs
concepts.body:
Bar graphs come in three common forms.

FormHow to read it
Simple barOne bar per year or item. Read the height against the axis.
Grouped (multiple) barsTwo or more bars side by side for each year, one per company or product. Use the legend to tell them apart.
Stacked barParts sit on top of each other. The height of a part is its top value minus its bottom value; the full bar is the total.

Check the scale: if the axis goes up in steps of 20 and a bar ends halfway between 60 and 80, its value is 70. When the value is printed on top of the bar, use that number rather than reading the axis.

concepts.title: Line graphs
concepts.body:
A line graph shows how a value changes over time. Each point is one reading; the line joining them only shows the trend.

  • The steeper the line between two years, the bigger the absolute change.
  • The biggest absolute rise is not always the biggest percentage rise. A rise from 20 to 30 is 50%, while a rise from 80 to 100 is only 25%.
  • Where two lines cross, the two values are equal. The gap between lines is the difference.

concepts.title: Pie charts
concepts.body:
A pie chart shows how a whole splits into parts. The full circle is 360° and stands for 100% of the total.

  • 1% of the total = 3.6°, so degrees = percent × 3.6.
  • Value of a sector = total × (angle ÷ 360) = total × (percent ÷ 100).
  • Comparing two sectors of the same pie needs no total: the ratio of values equals the ratio of angles or percents.
Percent5%10%12.5%15%20%25%30%33⅓%40%50%
Degrees18°36°45°54°72°90°108°120°144°180°

Mini example: in a pie of a ₹50 lakh budget, a 72° sector is 72 ÷ 360 = 1/5 of it, which is ₹10 lakh.

SSC often asks a pie question on a table: "If the data were shown as a pie chart, what is the central angle for X?" Then angle = (X ÷ total) × 360°.

concepts.title: The percentage toolkit
concepts.body:
Question wordingFormula
A is what percent of B?A ÷ B × 100
A is what percent more than B?(A − B) ÷ B × 100
A is what percent less than B?(B − A) ÷ B × 100
Percent increase from old to new(new − old) ÷ old × 100
Percent decrease from old to new(old − new) ÷ old × 100

The base (what you divide by) is always the value after "than", "of" or "from".

Percent versus percentage points. If a pass rate goes from 40% to 50%, it rose by 10 percentage points, but by 25% (10 ÷ 40 × 100).

Fractions to know by heart (they turn divisions into quick percentages):

Fraction1/31/61/71/81/91/111/121/151/16
Percent33.3316.6714.2912.511.119.098.336.676.25

Mini example: 18 ÷ 54 = 1/3, so a rise from 54 to 72 is 33⅓%.

concepts.title: Ratios and averages
concepts.body:
Ratio. Write the two numbers as a fraction and cancel common factors: 105 : 130, divide both by 5, gives 21 : 26. When both values are in the same unit you can ignore the unit.

Average. Average = total ÷ number of values. Count carefully: from 2019 to 2023 is 5 years, not 4.

Quick average by deviations. Pick a round value near the middle and average the differences. For 48, 52, 55 and 61, take 50: the differences are −2, +2, +5, +11, which add to 16. The average is 50 + 16 ÷ 4 = 54.

Average of averages. Only add averages directly when each group has the same size. Otherwise use totals.

concepts.title: Estimating and comparing fractions
concepts.body:
SSC options are often far apart, so you rarely need full division.

  • Round to friendly numbers: 49.8 ÷ 251 is about 50 ÷ 250 = 20%.
  • To find the larger of two fractions, cross-multiply: 13/17 versus 19/25 compares 13 × 25 = 325 with 19 × 17 = 323, so 13/17 is slightly larger.
  • To find the year with the highest percent growth, compare the ratios new ÷ old, not the raw differences.
  • When a question says "approximately", pick the nearest option after a rough calculation.

concepts.title: Derived values: profit, marks and more
concepts.body:
Some questions need a quantity that is not in the chart. Learn the common formulas:

Data givenQuantity askedFormula
Income I and expenditure EProfitI − E
Income I and expenditure EProfit percent(I − E) ÷ E × 100
Expenditure E and profit percent pIncomeE × (100 + p) ÷ 100
Students appeared and pass percentNumber passedappeared × pass% ÷ 100
Marks in percent and maximum marksMarks obtainedpercent × maximum ÷ 100
Exports and importsTrade surplus or deficitexports − imports

Mini example: income ₹84 lakh, expenditure ₹60 lakh. Profit = ₹24 lakh, profit percent = 24 ÷ 60 × 100 = 40%.

If a chart gives "percent profit" for two companies with equal expenditure, the one with the larger percent has the larger income. Without equal expenditure, you cannot compare incomes from percents alone.

varieties.name: Totals and differences
varieties.how: Write the needed values in a line, add them, and subtract only at the end. Keep the unit from the title.

example.q: Production (in thousand units) of two companies. P: 2020 = 45, 2021 = 60, 2022 = 54, 2023 = 72. Q: 2020 = 50, 2021 = 48, 2022 = 66, 2023 = 80. By how much did the total production of Q over the four years exceed that of P?

varieties.name: Average from data
varieties.how: Add the values and divide by how many there are. Count the years carefully.

example.q: Production (in thousand units) of two companies. P: 2020 = 45, 2021 = 60, 2022 = 54, 2023 = 72. Q: 2020 = 50, 2021 = 48, 2022 = 66, 2023 = 80. What is the average yearly production of Q?

varieties.name: What percent of, more or less than
varieties.how: The value after "than" or "of" is the base. Percent more = difference ÷ base × 100.

example.q: Production (in thousand units) of two companies. P: 2020 = 45, 2021 = 60, 2022 = 54, 2023 = 72. Q: 2020 = 50, 2021 = 48, 2022 = 66, 2023 = 80. In 2021, P's production was what percent more than Q's?

varieties.name: Percentage change over time
varieties.how: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100, where old is the earlier year. Use fraction values like 1/3 = 33⅓%.

example.q: Production (in thousand units) of two companies. P: 2020 = 45, 2021 = 60, 2022 = 54, 2023 = 72. Q: 2020 = 50, 2021 = 48, 2022 = 66, 2023 = 80. What is the percentage increase in P's production from 2022 to 2023?

varieties.name: Ratio from data
varieties.how: Find each side of the ratio (often a total), then divide both by their HCF.

example.q: Production (in thousand units) of two companies. P: 2020 = 45, 2021 = 60, 2022 = 54, 2023 = 72. Q: 2020 = 50, 2021 = 48, 2022 = 66, 2023 = 80. What is the ratio of P's total production in 2020 and 2021 to Q's production in 2020 and 2023 together?

varieties.name: Pie charts and central angles
varieties.how: The whole is 360° or 100%. Degrees = percent × 3.6, and a sector's value = total × angle ÷ 360.

example.q: A company spends ₹50 lakh. Salary takes 30% and transport takes a 72° sector of the pie chart. Find the central angle for salary and the amount spent on transport.

varieties.name: Highest, lowest and how many
varieties.how: Work out the measure asked for each year or item (often roughly), then pick or count. Do not compute exact values you do not need.

example.q: Production (in thousand units) of two companies. P: 2020 = 45, 2021 = 60, 2022 = 54, 2023 = 72. Q: 2020 = 50, 2021 = 48, 2022 = 66, 2023 = 80. In how many years was Q's production more than its own four-year average?

varieties.name: Derived values
varieties.how: Write the formula that links the shown data to the asked quantity (profit = income − expenditure, profit percent on expenditure), then substitute.

example.q: A company's income in 2023 was ₹84 lakh and its expenditure was ₹60 lakh. What was its profit percent?

tips: Read the title, units and legend before the first question. Write the unit beside your answer.
If two or more questions use the same totals, compute them once and note them beside the data.
Look at the options before calculating. When they are far apart, round and estimate.
Learn fraction-to-percent values (1/6 = 16.67%, 1/7 = 14.29%, 1/8 = 12.5%). They turn division into recall.
For pie charts, 1% = 3.6°. Comparing two sectors of one pie needs no total at all.
To find the highest percent growth, compare new ÷ old for each year, not the raw differences.
Count years inclusively: 2019 to 2023 is five years.
traps: "A is what percent less than B" divides by B, while "B is what percent more than A" divides by A. The two answers differ.
A rise of 10 percentage points is not a 10% rise. From 40% to 50% is a 25% rise.
The biggest jump on a line graph is the biggest absolute change, not always the biggest percent change.
In stacked bars, read a part as top minus bottom, not as the top value.
Check that both values are in the same unit (thousands versus lakhs, or percent versus actual numbers) before dividing.

passages.title: Production of Company X
passages.text: Study the bar chart and answer the questions. The chart shows the production of Company X (in thousand units) from 2019 to 2023: 2019 – 40, 2020 – 55, 2021 – 50, 2022 – 70, 2023 – 85.

What is the ratio of the sales of shop A to the sales of shop B in 2023?

What is the average sales per shop in 2022 (in ₹ lakh)?
